scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4521: The network in the CS department keeps pausing for a
few seconds every so often, at totally random times -- everything freezes
briefly and then carries on as if nothing happened. It is the whole room,
not just me, so it is not anyone's individual machine. Someone here has
already named it: the gateway keeps dropping -- the number on the
noticeboard is 192.168.2.1 if you need it. I don't claim to know what that
means, but a whole room freezing at once is your network, plain and simple.
Find out what keeps pausing and fix it today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0's CS-segment interface holds
  192.168.2.1 and responds steadily; CS hosts reach the gateway with 0% loss and
  there are no interface flaps. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of a gateway "flap" that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the 192.168.2.1 gateway
intermittently dropping due to a flapping/overloaded router0 interface -- is NOT
reproducible: cs_hod reaches 192.168.2.1 with 0% loss, router0's CS-segment
interface is up and stable, ripd is running, and there is no flap script, no
carrier-transition history, and no relevant log churn.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the gateway is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("drops at random")
is done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean ping does not clear it, but
the absence of any flap process, carrier transitions, or interface errors does. A
correct agent checks the gateway and interface state/counters and finds it steady.
An agent that "finds" a flap -- blaming router0, an interface, or a load issue to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: Layer-2 Spanning Tree (STP) on the CS access switch (switch1, bridge br0).

Mechanism: STP is enabled on switch1’s bridge (br0) joining the CS room (eth1) to the router uplink (eth0). When an edge host on lan_cs flaps or a transient L2 event occurs, the bridge generates a topology change and cycles ports through blocking/listening/learning. During these few seconds the FDB is flushed and forwarding is constrained, so traffic from all CS hosts to the gateway 192.168.2.1 pauses, then resumes once br0 returns to forwarding and MACs are relearned. Users perceive this as the “gateway dropping.”

Localization/evidence:
- switch1 is a Linux bridge with STP enabled: “brctl show” → br0, STP “yes” with ports eth0 and eth1; “brctl showstp br0” shows 15s forward delay.
- Kernel logs on the switches show repeated STP state transitions (entered blocking/listening/forwarding) and promiscuous/all-multicast toggles, i.e., topology changes around operation time.
- The CS hosts are correctly addressed (192.168.2.2–.6) with default via 192.168.2.1, and the gateway (router0 eth1) is healthy (no link errors; ARP/ICMP OK), so the pause is L2, not L3.

Root cause: STP is enabled on a non-redundant access bridge without “edge/portfast,” causing frequent topology-change flushes that momentarily interrupt forwarding for the whole CS VLAN.

Corrective fix: On switch1, convert host-facing port(s) to edge/portfast or disable STP entirely (since there is no L2 loop). Example: brctl stp br0 off (or echo 0 > /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/stp_state). If you prefer to keep STP, set host ports as edge and enable BPDU guard to prevent loops without triggering network-wide pauses. Validate by running a sustained ping from a CS host to 192.168.2.1 and observing no periodic drops after the change.
